content.english: About Kitāb al-Anwār wa-l-marāqib (The Book of Lights and Watchtowers)

The Kitāb al-Anwār wa-l-marāqib (The Book of Lights and Watchtowers) is the masterwork of Jacob al-Qirqisani, completed in 937 CE. This comprehensive treatise serves as both a systematic legal code and a work of biblical interpretation designed to guide Jewish religious practice.
Structure and Organization
The work is organized into thirteen discourses (maqālāt), each addressing different aspects of Jewish religious law, philosophy, and practice:
Discourses 1-2: Theological foundations, including discussions of sectarian groups within Judaism and principles of biblical interpretation
Discourse 3: Interreligious polemics, examining other religious traditions and defending Jewish positions
Discourse 4: Legal hermeneutics and methodology for deriving law from Scripture
Discourses 5-13: Systematic treatment of Jewish religious law, covering the practical commandments of the Torah in comprehensive detail

The legal discourses (5-13) form the core of the work, providing detailed guidance on Sabbath observance, festival celebrations, dietary laws, ritual purity, family relationships, inheritance, and commercial ethics.
Purpose and Methodology

Kitāb al-Anwār serves multiple functions: it is a comprehensive legal code, a work of biblical exegesis, a philosophical treatise, and a guide for religious practice. The work's title—"Lights and Watchtowers"—reflects its dual purpose: to illuminate the correct understanding of biblical law (lights) and to serve as lookout points for identifying and responding to religious controversies and challenges (watchtowers).

Al-Qirqisani approaches biblical interpretation through systematic analysis, employing logical argumentation, analogical reasoning, and careful textual examination. He frequently engages with opposing viewpoints, presenting their arguments before offering his own detailed refutations or alternative interpretations.
Scope of This Translation

This translation covers Discourses 5-13, which contain al-Qirqisani's commentary on the legal commandments of the Torah. These represent the most practically relevant sections for understanding how al-Qirqisani believed Jews should worship according to divine commandment. Discourses 3 and 4, while valuable for understanding his intellectual framework, remain untranslated in this edition.
Preface: From Nemoy's Edition to the Current Translation

When Leon Nemoy (1901–1997), a Russian-Jewish librarian at Yale University, embarked on his monumental project in the 1930s to reconstruct Yaʿqūb al-Qirqisānī's Kitāb al-Anwār wa-l-marāqib (The Book of Lights and Watchtowers), he was attempting a task nearly impossible: to piece together a highly-complex, lengthy text from what he described as "wretchedly fragmentary" manuscripts scattered across dozens of libraries worldwide. The early tenth-century Karaite scholar's magnum opus existed only in fragments—hundreds of unordered pages recovered from the Cairo Genizah. Based in the US, Nemoy had access only to photoscans of over 3,000 of these pages, a majority of which he managed to receive through his personal connections from the Russian National Library in St. Petersburg.

Nemoy's painstaking work, supported by the Alexander Kohut Memorial Foundation, spanned over a dozen years. What emerged was not merely a scholarly edition but a resurrection of a nearly-lost text—the recovery of what Nemoy himself called a "monumental thesaurus of tenth-century Karaite information." Published between 1939 and 1945, the five-volume "Nemoy edition" became the cornerstone for all subsequent research into medieval Karaite Judaism, including the vexing question over the "origins of Karaism." Since its publication, the Nemoy edition has provided scholars with unprecedented access to al-Qirqisānī's comprehensive treatment of Jewish law, philosophy, biblical interpretation, and interreligious polemics.
Decades Without Translation

For nearly eight decades following Nemoy's edition, a small group of scholars have published academic works based upon the Arabic text but planned efforts for a comprehensive English translation never succeeded. The exception was the Chiesa-Lockwood edition of the first two discourses, which provided a tantalizing glimpse into the richness of al-Qirqisānī's thought but left the vast majority of the work untranslated.

This gap was particularly significant given Nemoy's own recognition that "Karaite studies [has] always been neglected and [are the] unpopular stepchildren in the general field of Jewish history." While Nemoy had made important strides in popularizing Karaite studies through his Karaite Anthology (1952) and various translations of shorter works, the full scope of al-Qirqisānī's intellectual achievement remained hidden behind the language barrier.
A New Chapter Begins

The present translation represents the fulfillment of a long-held aspiration, shared by scholars and the broader Karaite community: to make al-Qirqisānī's masterpiece available to a wider audience via translation. Building upon a Hebrew-language translation completed by Yinon Kahan (PhD, Hebrew University), and fueled by rapid technological advances in artificial intelligence, this translation seeks to balance a faithful reading of the original Arabic text while remaining accessible to the contemporary reader by removing some jargon and technical vocabulary.

The current translation covers Volumes Three to Five of the Nemoy edition—Discourses 5-13 of al-Qirqisānī's work—specifically those sections containing his commentary on the legal commandments of the Torah. These discourses represent the heart of al-Qirqisānī's practical guidance for Jewish religious life, providing detailed analysis of how to properly worship God.

Two discourses therefore remain untranslated: Discourse 3 on interreligious polemics and Discourse 4 on the correct hermeneutics of deciding the law. While these are valuable for understanding al-Qirqisānī's intellectual framework, Discourses 5-13 contain the material most essential for understanding how al-Qirqisānī believed Jews should worship according to divine commandment.
A thematic glossary is also included at the conclusion of the introduction, for the reader's convenience. For more advanced study, we have preserved the original page numbering from Nemoy's edition.
Acknowledgments
This translation project was made possible through the generous support of the Binah Nemoy Memorial Fund, Yale University, as well as the following donors: [list of donors to be inserted].

This translation thus advances a journey that began in the fragments of the Cairo Genizah, passed through the devoted scholarship of Leon Nemoy, and now reaches contemporary students of Jewish history, law, and theology. What Nemoy rescued from obscurity, we now offer in translation of its most practically relevant sections—those that address the fundamental question of how to worship God according to Scripture. This work stands as a testament to the enduring power of scholarly dedication and the timeless relevance of al-Qirqisānī's guidance for religious life.
How to Use This Translation
This translation has been designed with multiple levels of engagement in mind, allowing readers to approach al-Qirqisānī's legal thought at whatever depth suits their interests and available time.
For Quick Reference: Chapter Summaries

If you're looking for the bottom line of al-Qirqisānī's legal positions on specific topics, start with the chapter summaries. These provide concise overviews of his main arguments, conclusions, and how they differ from other medieval authorities. Each summary distills pages of complex debates into accessible explanations, perfect for understanding his overall approach to Jewish law without getting wrapped up in layers of argumentation.
For Independent Study: Biblical Verses

Before diving into al-Qirqisānī's interpretations, we encourage you to engage with the source material yourself. Each chapter includes the relevant biblical verses in both Hebrew and English translation. Try reading these passages first to form your own understanding of what the text might mean. Then compare your reading with al-Qirqisānī's sophisticated analysis. This approach mirrors the Karaite emphasis on independent scriptural investigation while appreciating the insights of learned scholars.
For Deep Analysis: Full Chapter Translations

When you want to understand al-Qirqisānī's methodology, his responses to opponents, and the nuances of his legal reasoning, turn to the complete chapter translations. Here you'll find his systematic arguments, his citations of earlier authorities, and his innovative approaches to resolving legal disputes. These translations preserve the complexity of his thought while making it accessible to contemporary readers.
For Scholarly Mastery: The Original Arabic

For those seeking the deepest possible engagement with al-Qirqisānī's thought, consider studying classical Arabic to read his original text. While our translation strives for accuracy and readability, every translation involves interpretive choices. Reading the Arabic original allows you to appreciate the full subtlety of his language, his sophisticated use of Islamic legal terminology, and the precise way he constructs his arguments. Many universities offer courses in classical Arabic, and several online resources can help you begin this journey.
A Note on Practical Application

Remember that al-Qirqisānī wrote for his own time and circumstances. While his legal principles remain valuable for understanding Karaite thought, contemporary Karaite communities in many cases have evolved since the 10th century away from his conclusions. This translation serves primarily as a window into medieval Jewish legal reasoning and the development of Karaite jurisprudence, rather than as a definitive guide to practical Jewish observance.
I. Historical Context: The World of Tenth-Century Baghdad
Baghdad as Intellectual Center

The foundation of al-Mansur's 'Round City' of Baghdad in 762 CE marked a pivotal moment in world intellectual history. By the time Yaqub al-Qirqisani was active in the early 10th century, Baghdad had become what the 9th-century geographer Yaqubi described as "the crossroads of the universe." This remarkable city served as the cultural and intellectual center of the world, attracting pioneering scientists, astronomers, poets, mathematicians, musicians, historians, legal scholars, and philosophers from across the vast Islamic empire and beyond.

The period of al-Qirqisani's activity coincided with what scholar Joel Kraemer has termed the "Renaissance of Islam"—a classical revival and cultural flowering within Islamic civilization during the Buyid dynasty (934-1055 CE). This renaissance was particularly significant for Jewish intellectual life, given that the vast majority of worldwide Jewry during this period lived within the Abbasid Empire. Estimates suggest that around 80-90% of the world's Jewish population during the 10th century lived under Islamic rule, with the Babylonian Jewish community alone numbering around one million people.
The Islamic Renaissance and Jewish Communities
The Islamic renaissance profoundly affected Jewish communities and was characterized by several key features evident in al-Qirqisani's writings:

Philosophical Humanism: There was a conscious attempt to assimilate and transmit the intellectual legacy of Greek antiquity. Islamic and Jewish scholars embraced the scientific and philosophical heritage of the ancient world as a cultural and educational ideal, citing Arabic commentaries of Aristotle alongside traditional religious sources.
Literary Culture: Alongside philosophical inquiry, a literary humanism epitomized in the Arabic concept of adab (cultural refinement) flourished among litterateurs, poets, and government officials.

Cosmopolitanism: Baghdad was truly a microcosm of the Islamic world—a meeting place for scholars of diverse cultural, ethnic, and religious backgrounds. Philosophers considered themselves members of a universal intellectual class that transcended particular religious or ethnic loyalties.

Religious Challenge and Opportunity: The rise of independent philosophical inquiry fundamentally disrupted traditional religious authority. Religious leaders—whether Jewish, Christian, or Muslim—found themselves compelled to engage in systematic apologetics, developing sophisticated arguments to defend their faith claims both to skeptical members within their own communities and in competitive dialogue with other religious traditions.
The Majlis Culture

A key institution in this intellectual milieu was the majlis (plural: majālis)—salon-like scholarly sessions hosted by caliphs, emirs, viziers, or prominent scholars. These formal gatherings brought together scholars, philosophers, theologians, and representatives of different religious communities to participate in debates (jadal) and disputes (munazira) on literary, legal, and religious topics.

The majlis system facilitated what Shlomo Dov Goitein called "creative symbiosis"—cross-communal interaction among members of different religious groups in the Near East. Al-Qirqisani discusses the majlis several times in Kitab al-Anwar, noting that he expects his works to be discussed by his followers at the majlis, that he learned about the opinions of other Karaite religious scholars by attending these gatherings, and providing laws discussing the correct way to participate in such meetings.
Jewish Religious Diversity in Baghdad

The Jewish community in 10th-century Baghdad was far more complex and diverse than the traditional binary division between Rabbanites and Karaites would suggest. This religious complexity is captured in al-Qirqisani's observation that "at the present time disagreement between our co-religionists has greatly increased." The intellectual landscape was characterized by vigorous debate about interpretive methodology, the authority of tradition versus reasoned inquiry, and the proper relationship between religious texts and philosophical investigation.

Rabbanites accepted the authority of both the written Torah and the Oral Law as embodied in rabbinic literature. Led by the Geonim of the Babylonian academies, they issued responsa and maintained fidelity to the tradition of the Mishna and Talmud. The most prominent figure was Saadia Gaon (882-942), the influential head of the Sura academy who defended Rabbanite Judaism against Karaite challenges through both halakhic rulings and philosophical works.

Karaites rejected rabbinic oral tradition as authoritative and advocated for the Hebrew Bible as the sole revelatory text for determining religious law. Geographically dispersed and without centralized leadership, they were not monolithic and frequently disagreed among themselves. Key figures included Daniel al-Qumisi, a 9th-century scholar and mourner of Zion who wrote extensively on biblical exegesis from Jerusalem, and Benjamin al-Nahawandi, who developed influential legal methodologies and established communities in Persia.
Beyond these prominent named figures, he frequently quotes many anonymous Karaite leaders who, despite having smaller followings, contributed to the rich intellectual ferment.

Other sectarian groups proliferated beyond these main divisions. The Ananites followed Anan ben David (whom al-Qirqisani calls simply "The Exilarch"), the 8th-century founder whose creative exegetical methods influenced later Karaite thought. Groups led by a charismatic (often messianic) leader were not unusual at this time: al-Qirqisani documents several of these leaders, such as Isma'il al-'Ukbari, whose distinctive legal interpretations attracted followers, including his disciple Mishawayh al-'Ukbari. The latter developed a unique solar calendar system, and a full list of the innovative rulings attributed to each of these leaders is documented in the first discourse of al-Qirqisani’s Kitab al-Anwar (translated by Nemoy and Chiesa-Lockwood).

Additional sects include one founded by Abu 'Imran Musa al-Za'farani al-Tiflisi after emigrating from Iraq to Tiflis, the followers of Abu 'Isa al-Isfahani, and the Yudghaniyya—all described as small in number.

While al-Qirqisani describes a clear split in leadership between Rabbanites and Karaites, he also depicts a whole mass of "simple Jews" whose religious affiliation appears more mixed and fluid. It was precisely for these individuals—caught between competing religious authorities, in addition to Karaites disagreeing amongst themselves—that al-Qirqisani was arguably trying to win over rhetorically in his lengthy debates we have now translated.

While official Karaite-Rabbanite doctrine may have implied a sharper separation of the two communities, scholar Marina Rustow provided evidence from the Cairo Geniza that the medieval Egyptian community was much more fluid with shared marriage contracts, mutual synagogue attendance, and more.
Qirqisani: Life and Intellectual Position
Origins and Identity

Jacob al-Qirqisani (Arabic: Abū Yūsuf Yaʻqūb ibn Isḥāq ibn Samaʻwayh al-Qirqisānī) stands as one of the most prominent Karaite intellectuals of the 10th century and is considered by some as the "greatest Karaite scholar" of all time. Despite his significance, biographical details about his life remain sparse and fragmentary. His full name reveals his patronymic lineage (his father was Isaac, son of Samawayh), while his nisba (attributive name) "al-Qirqisānī" indicates a connection to Qarqisiyyah (the ancient town of Circesium), located on the eastern bank of the Euphrates near its confluence with the Khābūr River in what is now modern Syria.
Intellectual Formation and Career

While we lack direct evidence about Qirqisani's formal education, his writings reveal a man of exceptional erudition and intellectual breadth. Some of his writings suggest travels to Persia and India, which would have exposed him to diverse philosophical, religious, and cultural traditions beyond the Jewish world.

His work demonstrates extensive knowledge of multiple languages and literary traditions. He was clearly fluent in Arabic and Hebrew, with evidence suggesting familiarity with Aramaic as well. His knowledge of Greek philosophical traditions, while likely acquired through Arabic translations, was nonetheless substantial.

The most certain date we have for Qirqisani's career is 937 CE, the year he completed his magnum opus, the Kitāb al-Anwār waʼl-Marāqib (Book of Lights and Watchtowers). This places him firmly in the intellectual milieu of early 10th century Baghdad during the "Renaissance of Islam" under Buyid rule.
Qirqisani as a Polymath

Qirqisani's surviving works demonstrate expertise in multiple domains: law and jurisprudence, biblical exegesis, philosophy and theology, philology and linguistics, heresiography, and comparative religion. This intellectual versatility places Qirqisani in the tradition of medieval polymaths who moved comfortably across disciplines, seeing knowledge as an integrated whole rather than discrete fields of specialization.
Intellectual Position Within the Karaite Community

Qirqisani occupied a distinctive position within 10th-century Karaism. While firmly committed to core Karaite principles—particularly the rejection of rabbinic oral tradition and emphasis on independent scriptural interpretation—he carved out a unique methodological approach that distinguished him from his predecessors.

His relationship to earlier Karaite authorities was complex. He criticized Anan ben David's "preposterous interpretations" while acknowledging him for establishing the principle of ḥippus (rational investigation of scripture). He dedicated considerable attention to examining Benjamin al-Nahawandi's distinctive positions, and maintained a similarly critical yet respectful stance toward Daniel al-Qumisi.

Qirqisani's emphasis on rational inquiry and his integration of philosophical methodology into biblical interpretation represented a sophisticated evolution in Karaite thought. While he was apparently unaware of the contemporaneous Jerusalem Karaite school, later Jerusalem Karaites like Japheth ben Eli knew and engaged with his work, suggesting his influence extended beyond his immediate circle.
Qirqisani's Major Works

Jacob al-Qirqisani's intellectual contributions are primarily known to us through his two monumental works: the Kitāb al-Anwār wa'l-Marāqib (Book of Lights and Watchtowers) and the Kitāb al-Riyāḍ wa'l-Ḥadā'iq (Book of Gardens and Parks). These comprehensive compositions, serve as the foundation for our understanding of his thought. The former stands as a massive legal-theological summa, while the latter constitutes an extensive commentary on the non-legal portions of the Torah.

Beyond these major works, Qirqisani authored several shorter treatises that are unfortunately lost to us today. We know of their existence only through references he made to them in his two surviving major works. These earlier compositions demonstrate the remarkable breadth of his intellectual interests and scholarly activity:
Tafsīr Bēreshit - A commentary on Genesis
Tafsīr Iyob - A commentary on the Book of Job
Tafsīr Kohelet - A commentary on Ecclesiastes
Kitāb fī 'ifsād nubuwwat Muḥammad - A treatise refuting Muhammad's claim to prophecy
al-Ḳaul 'alā l-tafsīr wa-sharḥ al-ma'ānī - An essay on the art of textual interpretation
al-Ḳaul 'alā l-tarjama - An essay on the art of translation
Kitāb al-tauḥīd - A treatise on the oneness of God

This list may not represent Qirqisani's complete literary output up to 938, as he may have written other works that he had no occasion to mention. The scope of his known writings and the extensive nature of his two major works testify to his extraordinary industry and encyclopedic learning.

The range of subjects covered in these works—biblical exegesis, theology, legal theory, linguistic theory, hermeneutics, and comparative religion—reveals Qirqisani as a polymath whose intellectual horizons extended far beyond the boundaries of traditional Jewish learning. His sophisticated engagement with Islamic theological concepts, his methodical approach to textual interpretation, and his willingness to engage critically with both rabbinic and Karaite predecessors mark him as one of the most significant Jewish thinkers of the medieval Islamic world.
Case Study: Al-Qirqisani's Defense of Corpse Impurity in Exile

Having established the rich intellectual context of tenth-century Baghdad and al-Qirqisani's position within the diverse landscape of medieval Jewish thought, we now turn to examine his methodological approach through a concrete example. The following case study demonstrates how al-Qirqisani applied his sophisticated legal reasoning to resolve one of the most contentious debates within the Karaite community of his time.
The Legal Controversy

In chapters 55-56 of the 10th discourse of Kitāb al-Anwār, al-Qirqisani addresses a fundamental question that had sharply divided Karaite scholars: whether the biblical laws concerning corpse impurity (ṭumʾat met) remain binding during the exile period when the Temple no longer stands and the red heifer ashes required for purification water are unavailable. This controversy exemplifies the broader challenges facing Jewish communities in the Islamic world—how to maintain fidelity to scriptural commandments while adapting to the practical realities of life in exile.

The dispute centered on a seemingly insurmountable problem: When the biblical means of purification from corpse impurity—the "waters of sprinkling" prepared from the ashes of the red heifer described in Numbers 19—are no longer available, does the impurity itself remain binding? This question went to the heart of Jewish religious practice, affecting everything from burial customs to family relationships to participation in communal worship.
The Opposing Positions
Al-Qirqisani identifies two fundamentally different approaches to this dilemma:

Anan ben David's position: The founder of Ananism argued that corpse impurity should be abolished entirely in exile because purification via the red heifer ashes had become impossible. Anan's followers reasoned that since one could not fulfill the purification requirements explicitly mentioned in Numbers 19:12-13, the impurity itself was effectively nullified. This represented a pragmatic approach that prioritized implementability over theoretical obligation.

Al-Qirqisani's position: Corpse impurity remains fully binding in exile, and purification can be achieved through water immersion alone when the red heifer ashes are unavailable. This approach sought to preserve the fundamental structure of biblical law while providing practical guidance for observant Jews.
Al-Qirqisani's Methodological Innovation

What distinguishes al-Qirqisani's approach from that of his predecessors is his systematic application of four interconnected methodological principles that reflect the sophisticated intellectual culture of tenth-century Baghdad:
1. Structural Analysis of Legal Categories

Drawing upon concepts that likely reflect his familiarity with Islamic legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh), al-Qirqisani demonstrates sophisticated juridical reasoning by distinguishing between "root" (aṣl) and "branch" (farʿ) elements of the law. He argues that impurity constitutes the fundamental principle, while the specific purification method represents a derivative application:

"Necessarily, impurity from the dead is the root [of the law] and the waters of sprinkling are its branch... It is not possible for the root to be nullified because the branch was nullified, but necessarily [the opposite is correct]—the branch is nullified because of the nullification of the root."

This hierarchical conception of legal principles represents a significant methodological innovation in Jewish jurisprudence, demonstrating how al-Qirqisani integrated contemporary Arabic-Islamic intellectual frameworks while remaining firmly grounded in biblical exegesis.
2. Analogical Reasoning (Qiyās)

Al-Qirqisani employs systematic analogical reasoning to demonstrate that other forms of ritual impurity remain binding despite the absence of Temple sacrifices. His analysis reveals the underlying consistency of the biblical purification system:

"Similarly, the law of waters of sprinkling for a corpse-impure person is like the law of 'two birds and cedar-wood, and scarlet, and hyssop' for a leper. And just as the leper is not purified except with water, even if he has done all the [other] things [mentioned in the verse], so too a corpse-impure person is not purified except with water, even if waters of sprinkling were sprinkled upon him."

Through this parallel, al-Qirqisani establishes that water immersion serves as the fundamental purification method when Temple-dependent elements are unavailable—a solution that maintains legal coherence without imposing impossible requirements on Jews in exile.
3. Contextual Textual Interpretation

Al-Qirqisani demonstrates his exegetical sophistication by reinterpreting biblical verses that his opponents had used to support their position. When addressing Numbers 19:13 ("because the water of sprinkling was not dashed against him, he remains unclean"), he argues:

"His words 'because the water of sprinkling was not dashed against him, he remains unclean' are binding when there is possibility and existence [of the thing]. However, when the thing is absent and not available, there is no death penalty and the impurity does not remain."

This interpretive approach allows him to maintain the binding nature of corpse impurity while recognizing that unavailability of certain purification rituals does not result in permanent impurity—a nuanced reading that balances textual fidelity with practical implementation.
4. Distinction Between Intent and Capability
Perhaps most innovative is al-Qirqisani's introduction of a principle that accounts for human intention and circumstantial capability:

"If it is [the first case] and nothing prevented them, rather they neglected the commandment and intended to violate it, they will never achieve purification and are liable to death... [But] if death does not obligate when they refrain [from sprinkling] on the third and seventh days [due to impossibility] then on other days it certainly will not obligate."

In this section, al-Qirqisani distinguishes between one who fails to perform the rituals to be cleansed of corpse impurity when it is possible, with one who is unable to perform these rituals. The former is liable for the death penalty, while the latter cannot be punished as such since it is impossible for him to act otherwise.
Implications for Jewish Life in Exile
Al-Qirqisani's resolution of the corpse impurity controversy carries profound implications that extend far beyond the specific legal question at hand:

Theological coherence: His approach preserves the integrity of the biblical legal system by maintaining its fundamental structure while adapting implementation to exilic conditions. This demonstrates how Jewish law could remain both divinely authoritative and practically relevant in the diaspora.

Practical guidance: By establishing that water immersion alone suffices when red heifer ashes are unavailable, he provides a concrete path for observant Jews to maintain ritual purity without access to Temple-based purification methods.

Legal methodology: His clear distinction between willful violation and inability to perform commandments due to circumstances becomes a model for legal reasoning that could be applied to other areas where exile conditions created similar implementation challenges.
Conclusion

Al-Qirqisani's treatment of corpse impurity laws exemplifies the intellectual sophistication he brought to Jewish legal thought. By combining rigorous textual analysis with logical argumentation and sensitivity to practical implementation, he developed a framework that balanced scriptural fidelity with the realities of Jewish existence in the Islamic world.

This case study reveals how al-Qirqisani's methodology was simultaneously conservative and innovative—conservative in its unwavering commitment to biblical commandments, yet innovative in its sophisticated analytical techniques drawn from the broader intellectual culture of his time. His willingness to engage directly with his opponents' strongest arguments while developing coherent alternative frameworks reflects the vibrant intellectual climate of tenth-century Baghdad and the creative possibilities that emerged from the encounter between Jewish tradition and Islamic civilization.

The principles al-Qirqisani develops in this controversy—the hierarchical understanding of legal categories, systematic analogical reasoning, contextual interpretation, and the distinction between intent and capability—would influence subsequent generations of Karaite scholars and contribute to the broader development of Jewish jurisprudence. His approach demonstrates how religious law could maintain its divine authority while adapting to the practical challenges of diaspora existence, offering a model for Jewish legal thinking that remains relevant across different historical circumstances.
Glossary of Technical Terms:
Sabbath Observance

Avot Melakhot (אבות מלאכות) - "Categories of work." The Rabbinic concept of 39 primary categories of work prohibited on the Sabbath. Al-Qirqisani critiques this categorization while discussing various prohibited activities.

'Asiyah (עשייה) - "General actions" or "activities." Non-professional activities distinguished from melakha (skilled labor). Includes everyday physical movements such as "walking and standing and sitting and sleeping and eating and drinking" and also the opposites of skilled labors, such as "unraveling which is the opposite of weaving, and tearing which is the opposite of tailoring."

Bi'ur (ביעור) - "Lighting" or "burning." The term has dual meanings: the initial action of lighting a fire and the continued burning of the fire. This distinction is crucial for understanding Sabbath fire prohibitions.
Chol (חול) - "Weekday" or "profane day." Any day that is not the Sabbath or a holiday; a regular day without special religious significance.

Hachanah (הכנה) - "Preparation." The concept of preparing food and other necessities before the Sabbath for use on the Sabbath. Al-Qirqisani debates the extent of required preparation, noting different interpretations of Exodus 16:5.

Mavir (מבעיר) - "One who kindles." The person who lights a fire. Important in discussions about whether someone who lit a fire before the Sabbath is considered to be "burning" on the Sabbath if the fire continues.

Melakha (מלאכה) - "Skilled labor" or "professional work" or "craft." A category of work prohibited on the Sabbath that involves specialized skills or professions, such as weaving, building, or writing. Distinguished from general activities ('asiyah). Al-Qirqisani defines melakha as work related to recognized professions "like a silversmith and carpenter and tailor and weaver and welder and trader and perfumer."

Oneg (עונג) - "Delight." The concept of enjoying the Sabbath, referenced in Isaiah 58:13. The text discusses whether various activities, including marital relations, constitute proper Sabbath delight.

Reshut (רשות) - "Domain" or "property" or "area." A legal category of space that determines what activities are permitted. Important in discussions of Sabbath boundaries and prohibitions on carrying objects between different types of domains.

Shamor/Zakhor (שמור/זכור) - "Observe/Remember." The dual commandments regarding Sabbath observance. Al-Qirqisani explains that "'remember' means to remember the Sabbath before its appearance to be concerned with it and safeguard that there be no negligence or carelessness, and 'observe' means to protect the Sabbath once it has begun."
Shabbaton (שבתון) - "Solemn rest." A complete cessation of work, referring to the special character of the Sabbath as a day of rest.

Techumin (תחומין) - "Sabbath domain" or "designated Sabbath area." The limits within which one may travel on the Sabbath. The text discusses different interpretations of these boundaries, including the view that one cannot leave one's town or village on the Sabbath.
Toldot (תולדות) - "Derivatives." Secondary prohibited activities derived from the primary categories of work. Al-Qirqisani discusses whether "derivative actions" are prohibited on the Sabbath.
Calendar and Festivals

Aviv (אביב) - "Spring" or "green ears." The state of ripened barley that determines the first month. Karaites use the ripening of barley in the Land of Israel to determine the beginning of the year. Referenced in Deuteronomy 16:1: "Observe the month of Aviv and keep the Passover."

Ben Ha'Arvayim (בין הערביים) - "Between the evenings." The time period decreed for slaughtering the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:6). According to many Karaites, this period begins at sunset and ends at the complete disappearance of light (twilight), and is partially included in both the ending day and the beginning of the following day.

Boker (בוקר) - "Morning." Has three meanings: before dawn but close to it, the period from dawn to sunrise, and sunrise itself. Understanding these distinctions clarifies the proper times for morning offerings and prayers.

Carmel (כרמל) - "Fresh grain" or "new kernels." Describes the state of ripened grain that still contains moisture. Mentioned in Leviticus 2:14: "fresh ears parched with fire, crushed new grain (carmel)." Used to determine the proper time for the first month.

Chag HaMatzot (חג המצות) - "Festival of Unleavened Bread." The seven-day festival beginning on the fifteenth of the first month. The text discusses how this relates to the Passover sacrifice and the counting of weeks.

Chodesh (חודש) - "Month" or "new moon." The Hebrew term for both the lunar month and the new moon itself. The term appears in Exodus 12:2: "This month (chodesh) shall be unto you the beginning of months."

Erev (ערב) - "Evening." Has three meanings in Scripture: the moment of sunset, the twilight period between sunset and complete darkness, and the beginning of the night. Understanding these distinctions helps determine the proper time for offering sacrifices.

Intercalation (עיבור, ibbur) - The addition of a thirteenth month to synchronize the lunar year with the agricultural seasons. Based on the command to observe Passover in the month of Aviv (Exodus 13:4, Deuteronomy 16:1).

Mechalhel Be'Kharmel (מכלה בכרמל) - "When the sickle begins to cut the standing grain." The phrase from Deuteronomy 16:9 that some Karaites interpret as indicating when the counting of weeks should begin, related to the natural agricultural cycle rather than a fixed date.

Mikra Kodesh (מקרא קודש) - "Holy Convocation." A day set apart for assembly and rest from normal work. Applied to festival days including the first and seventh days of Unleavened Bread. From Leviticus 23:7: "on the first day shall be a holy convocation."

Mimmochorat HaShabbat (ממחרת השבת) - "The morrow of the Sabbath." The phrase in Leviticus 23:15 that Karaites interpret as the day after the weekly Sabbath (Sunday), on which the Omer offering should be performed. This interpretation determines when the counting of seven weeks begins for Shavuot.

Molad (מולד) - "Conjunction" or "birth." Refers to the astronomical conjunction of the sun and moon. Some groups argued this should determine the new month rather than the visible crescent. Not directly mentioned in the Bible, but supporters cited Genesis 1:14: "let them be for signs and for seasons."

Neshef (נשף) - "Twilight." The period between sunset and the complete disappearance of light. A crucial time for determining when festivals begin and end, and when the Passover lamb should be slaughtered. Possibly derived from the concept of "between the settings" - between the setting of the sun and the setting of light.

Omer (עומר) - The "sheaf" of the first harvest of barley that is waved as an offering. Karaites maintain this must be performed on the Sunday that falls during the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Based on Leviticus 23:10-11: "When you come into the land which I give you and reap its harvest, you shall bring the Omer of the first of your harvest to the priest."

Pesach (פסח) - "Passover." Specifically refers to the sacrifice offered on the fourteenth of the first month "between the evenings." According to the text, this is distinct from the Festival of Unleavened Bread that begins on the fifteenth. The text mentions that there are "three times" of Passover: the time of slaughter on the fourteenth, the time of eating on the fifteenth at night, and the time of "passing over" at midnight. Based on Exodus 12:6: "the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall slaughter it at twilight."

Re'iyah (ראייה) - "Sighting" or "observation." The visual sighting of the new moon crescent to determine the beginning of the month. While not explicitly commanded in those terms, Karaites derive this from passages like Numbers 28:14, referring to "the new moon in its renewal."

Reshit HaKatzir (ראשית הקציר) - "First of the harvest." Refers to the beginning of the barley harvest, which according to some Karaites determines when the Omer should be waved. Based on Leviticus 23:10: "you shall bring the sheaf of the first of your harvest to the priest."

Shabbatot Temimot (שבתות תמימות) - "Complete Sabbaths." The phrase from Leviticus 23:15 referring to the seven Sabbaths/weeks that must be counted between the waving of the Omer and Shavuot. Karaites interpret this to mean seven complete weeks ending with the weekly Sabbath.

Shavuot (שבועות) - "Festival of Weeks" or "Eid al-Ansara" as called by the public. The festival occurring on the fiftieth day after the waving of the Omer. Karaites believe it must always fall on Sunday. Based on Leviticus 23:15-16: "And you shall count for yourselves from the morrow of the Sabbath...until the morrow of the seventh Sabbath shall you count fifty days."

Yom (יום) - "Day." The text discusses ten different meanings of "day" in Scripture, primarily distinguishing between the "solar day" (from sunset to sunset) and the "day of light" (from dawn until twilight). Understanding these distinctions is crucial for determining festival observances.

Yom HaBikkurim (יום הבכורים) - "Day of First Fruits." Another name for Shavuot, referring to the offering of the first fruits of the wheat harvest. From Numbers 28:26: "on the day of first fruits, when you bring a new meal offering to the Lord in your Festival of Weeks."
Yom Kippur (יום כיפור) - "Day of Atonement." A holy day on which the Karaites observe fasting and specific prayers for atonement of sins.

Yom Teruah (יום תרועה) - "Day of Shouting/Blasting." The festival on the first day of the seventh month (Tishri), which Rabbanites call Rosh Hashanah. For Karaites, this is a day of shouting or trumpet blasting, as commanded in Leviticus 23:24: "a memorial proclaimed with the blast of horns, a holy convocation."
Yom Tov (יום טוב) - "Festival day" or "holy convocation." Biblical festivals established in Leviticus 23. Karaites debate whether these should be observed for one or two days.
Ritual Purity and Impurity

Emtza'i (אמצעי) - "Intermediary" or medium through which impurity is transmitted. Al-Qirqisani debates whether impurity can be transmitted through intermediaries or only through direct contact. No specific biblical verse, but discussed in relation to Leviticus 15 and Numbers 19.

Karet (כרת) - "Being cut off" or "spiritual excision." A severe divine punishment mentioned for certain transgressions, including failing to circumcise. The text notes that "one who is uncircumcised is obligated in death" (karet).
Keri (קרי) - Seminal emission that causes one-day impurity requiring washing and bathing. Based on Leviticus 15:16-18.

Mayim Chayim (מים חיים) - "Living water" required for purification from certain impurities. Karaites debated whether this meant spring water, cold water, or sweet water. Based on Leviticus 15:13 and Numbers 19:17.
Me Niddah (מי נדה) - "Waters of separation" or "water of sprinkling," prepared with ashes of the red heifer for purification from corpse impurity. Based on Numbers 19:9-13.
Merkav (מרכב) - A riding implement used by a ritually impure person (like a zav), which becomes impure and can transmit impurity to others. Based on Leviticus 15:9.
Metzora (מצורע) - Person afflicted with skin disease, often mistranslated as "leper." The text discusses shaving the head of the metzora and whether this can be done on the Sabbath.
Mishkav (משכב) - The bed or that which is lain upon by someone with impurity (like a zav or niddah), which then becomes impure and can transmit impurity to others. Based on Leviticus 15:4-5.
Moshav (מושב) - The seat used by someone with impurity (like a zav or niddah), which becomes impure and can transmit impurity to others. Based on Leviticus 15:6.
Nazir (נזיר) - One who has taken a Nazirite vow. Mentioned in discussions of shaving prohibitions and whether these can be performed on the Sabbath.

Niddah (נדה) - Ritual impurity related to menstruation. The text references "water of niddah" in discussions of purification rituals and their application on the Sabbath. A menstruating woman who is ritually impure for seven days. This impurity is transferred to items she sits or lies upon and to those who touch her. Based on Leviticus 15:19-24.

Nevela/Neveilah (נבלה) - An animal that died naturally (not through proper slaughter), causing impurity to those who touch or carry it. Based on Leviticus 11:39-40. "Carcass" or "carrion." An animal that died naturally without proper ritual slaughter. Al-Qirqisani distinguishes this from tereifah.

Ohel (אהל) - A tent or covering under which a corpse imparts ritual impurity to all present. Al-Qirqisani argues this specifically refers to an actual tent, not a house or permanent structure. Based on Numbers 19:14.
Sheretz (שרץ) - Creeping things (like mice, lizards) that cause ritual impurity when dead. Al-Qirqisani discusses the "eight creeping things" that convey impurity. Based on Leviticus 11:29-38.

Tzamid Patil (צמיד פתיל) - A tightly sealed cover for vessels that prevents impurity from entering when in the presence of a corpse. Karaites debated whether this refers to a thread binding or a complete wrapping. Based on Numbers 19:15.

Zav (זב) - A man with an abnormal genital discharge, considered ritually impure and requiring specific purification procedures. Based on Leviticus 15:2-15. Person with genital discharge. Individuals in a state of ritual impurity due to genital discharges, whose purification process is discussed in relation to Sabbath laws.

Zavah (זבה) - A woman with an abnormal discharge that continues beyond her regular menstrual period, requiring special purification procedures. Distinguished from regular menstruation (niddah). Based on Leviticus 15:25-30. Person with genital discharge. Individuals in a state of ritual impurity due to genital discharges, whose purification process is discussed in relation to Sabbath laws.
Dietary Laws and Forbidden Foods

Behemah (בהמה) - "Domesticated animal." Used in biblical passages to designate domesticated animals as opposed to wild ones, though al-Qirqisani notes that sometimes the term can apply more broadly to all animals. Source: Deuteronomy 14:4, "These are the animals [behemah] which you may eat: the ox, the sheep of lambs..."

Chayah (חיה) - "Wild animal" or more broadly "living thing." Al-Qirqisani explains that while this sometimes specifically refers to wild animals as distinct from domesticated ones (behemah), both terms can be used interchangeably depending on context. Source: Leviticus 11:2, "These are the living things [chayah] which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth."

Chelev (חלב) - "Fat." Specifically refers to the prohibited fat portions of animals. Al-Qirqisani identifies five forbidden fats in cattle and goats, plus a sixth (the tail) in sheep. Source: Leviticus 3:17, "All fat [chelev] and all blood you shall not eat."

Gid HaNashe (גיד הנשה) - "Sciatic nerve." The prohibition against eating the sciatic nerve of animals, which al-Qirqisani notes was not formally included in Moses' commandments but was transmitted through tradition due to the story of Jacob. Source: Genesis 32:33 (implied).

Kilayim (כלאים) - "Diverse kinds" or "mixtures." Refers to several biblical prohibitions: breeding different species of animals together, sowing different kinds of seeds together, and wearing garments of mixed fibers. Source: Leviticus 19:19, "You shall not let your cattle breed with diverse kinds [kilayim]."

Lo Tevashel Gedi (לא תבשל גדי) - "You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk." A commandment that al-Qirqisani interprets literally, rejecting the Rabbanite expansion that forbids all meat and milk combinations. Source: Exodus 23:19, "You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk."

Ma'aseh Goyim (מעשה גוים) - "Acts of gentiles." The Karaite debate over whether food prepared by non-Jews is permitted, which al-Qirqisani discusses extensively, generally arguing against the strict position that would forbid such food. No specific biblical source, but discussed in relation to Daniel 1:8-16.

Melika (מליקה) - "Neck-breaking." The method prescribed for ritual slaughter of birds designated for sacrifice. Al-Qirqisani debates whether this method is required for all birds or only sacrificial ones. Source: Leviticus 5:8, "and shall pinch off its head from opposite its neck [mimul orpo]."

Mul (מול) - "Opposite" or "adjoining." A term whose definition is debated in the context of bird slaughter (melika). Al-Qirqisani argues that it refers to the boundary of the thing itself, not something opposite or facing it. Source: Leviticus 5:8, "from opposite [mimul] his neck."

Orlah (ערלה) - "Forbidden fruit." The prohibition against eating fruit from newly planted trees during their first three years. Source: Leviticus 19:23, "Three years shall it be as forbidden [orlah] to you; it shall not be eaten."

Shechita (שחיטה) - "Slaughter." The method of ritual slaughtering animals by cutting the throat, which al-Qirqisani notes is inherently understood within the language without need for explanation. Also called "zevicha" (זביחה). Source: Leviticus 1:5 (shachat) and Exodus 20:24 (zavacht).

Sha'atnez (שעטנז) - "Mixed fibers." The biblical prohibition against wearing garments containing both wool and linen together. Karaites debate whether this extends to other animal/plant fiber combinations. Source: Leviticus 19:19, "Neither shall there come upon you a garment of diverse kinds [sha'atnez]."

Shivuot V'Yovelot (שביעית ויובלות) - "Sabbatical and Jubilee years." The seventh and fiftieth years in which the land must rest and various agricultural prohibitions apply. Al-Qirqisani notes these apply only in the Land of Israel. Source: Leviticus 25:2-4.

Tereifah/Trefa (טריפה) - "Torn animal." An animal that died due to being attacked by predators or another cause. Distinguished from neveilah which died naturally. Source: Exodus 22:30, "And flesh torn in the field [tereifah] you shall not eat."
Family, Marriage, and Inheritance

Ahuba (אהובה) - "Beloved wife." The favored wife in a polygamous marriage, whose son cannot be given preference in inheritance over the Leftful firstborn son of the less-favored wife. Source: Deuteronomy 21:15, "one beloved [ahuba], and another hated."

Bat Yoresheh Nachalah (בת יורשת נחלה) - "Daughter who possesses an inheritance." A daughter who inherits her father's property when he has no sons. According to Karaite law, such a daughter must marry within her father's tribe to prevent property transfer between tribes. Source: Numbers 36:8, "And every daughter, that possesseth an inheritance in any tribe of the children of Israel, shall be wife unto one of the family of the tribe of her father."

Bechor/Bekhor (בכור) - "Firstborn." The firstborn son who is entitled to receive a double portion of inheritance. Al-Qirqisani discusses the debate about whether this refers to the father's firstborn (first of his strength) or the mother's firstborn (first to open the womb). Source: Deuteronomy 21:17, "But he shall acknowledge the firstborn... and give him a double portion of all that he hath."
Beit Av (בית אב) - "House of the father." The patrilineal family unit that serves as the basis for inheritance. Source: Numbers 1:2, "after their families, by the house of their fathers."
Brit (ברית) - "Covenant." Particularly important in discussions of circumcision, which is described as "a covenant between us and God and a circumcision of the flesh."

Em V'et B'nah (אותו ואת בנו) - "It and its young." The prohibition against slaughtering a mother animal and its offspring on the same day. Source: Leviticus 22:28, "And whether it be ox or sheep, you shall not kill it and its young both in one day."

Goral (גורל) - "Lot." The method prescribed for dividing inheritance fairly, particularly regarding land division. Al-Qirqisani explains this prevents disputes and ensures fairness. Source: Numbers 26:55, "Notwithstanding the land shall be divided by lot [goral]."
Kadesh (קדש) - "Male prostitute" or "sodomite." A man who behaves like a woman and abandons himself to others for prostitution. Prohibited in Israelite society (Deuteronomy 23:18).
Kedeshah (קדשה) - "Sacred prostitute" or "harlot." A woman who makes herself available for prostitution for payment. Prohibited in Israelite society (Deuteronomy 23:18).

Mamzer (ממזר) - One born through a forbidden relationship that was entered into intentionally. Such a person was restricted from entering "the congregation" to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:2-3). According to the Karaite sage Jacob ben Reuben there were seven possibilities for the meaning of this word, including: heretical converts; one whose mother is known but whose father is unknown; one who is the offspring of forbidden sexual relations; one who is conceived during niddah; the name of a specific foreign nation; all converts; and "they who are not from the seed of Abraham."

Mateh (מטה) - "Tribe." Important in Karaite inheritance law, as the Torah prohibits the transfer of inherited land from one tribe to another. Source: Numbers 36:9, "Neither shall the inheritance remove from one tribe to another tribe."

Mattan (מתן) - "Gift." Property given during the testator's lifetime, which is distinct from inheritance. Al-Qirqisani notes that while a person cannot change inheritance laws, they can give gifts during their lifetime as they wish. Source: Genesis 25:6, "But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts [mattanot]."

Mi-Banim (מבנים) - "Above the sons." Al-Qirqisani's principle that parents inherit before children in the inheritance order, contrary to some interpretations. He argues this based on reason and Scripture. No direct biblical source, but implied from various passages.

Mishpachah (משפחה) - "Family." In inheritance contexts, refers specifically to the patrilineal family line. Al-Qirqisani notes that inheritance passes through the father's family, not the mother's. Source: Numbers 27:11, "unto his kinsman that is next to him of his family [mishpachto]."

Mohar (מהר) - "Bride-price." The payment given for marrying a woman. The standard bride-price for virgins was fifty shekels of silver in cases of forced marriage (Deuteronomy 22:29), though the amount could vary based on agreement between parties.

Nachalah (נחלה) - "Inheritance" or "possession." The transfer of property from a deceased person to their heirs according to biblical law. Al-Qirqisani notes that while biblical inheritance primarily focuses on land/estates, the principles apply to all property. Source: Numbers 27:8, "If a man die, and have no son, then ye shall cause his inheritance to pass unto his daughter."

Pi Shnayim (פי שניים) - "Double portion." The inheritance Left of the firstborn son to receive twice as much as each of his brothers. Al-Qirqisani notes this practice predates Mosaic law, evidenced by Jacob's purchase of Esau's birthLeft. Source: Deuteronomy 21:17, "by giving him a double portion [pi shnayim] of all that he hath."

Reshit Ono (ראשית אונו) - "Beginning of strength." A term used to describe the firstborn son who receives the double portion. Al-Qirqisani argues this refers to the first offspring from the father's loins rather than the firstborn of the womb. Source: Deuteronomy 21:17, "for he is the beginning of his strength [reshit ono]."

She'er Karov (שאר קרוב) - "Near kinsman" or "close relative." The term used to describe the next in line to inherit when more immediate heirs don't exist. Source: Numbers 27:11, "unto his kinsman that is next to him [she'ero hakarov] of his family."

Shenua (שנואה) - "Hated wife." In the context of inheritance laws, refers not to a wife who is truly hated but to one who is less favored than another wife. Al-Qirqisani notes that her firstborn son still receives the double portion regardless of the father's preferences. Source: Deuteronomy 21:15-17, "If a man have two wives, one beloved, and another hated [shenua]..."
Sotah (סוטה) - "Suspected adulteress." A woman suspected of adultery who undergoes a ritual test to determine her guilt or innocence (Numbers 5:12-31).

Tsava'ah (צוואה) - Though not explicitly mentioned by this term, the concept of a will or testament is discussed. Al-Qirqisani argues against the validity of wills that attempt to change the biblical inheritance order after death, as the property is no longer the testator's to control.

Yefat To'ar (יפת תואר) - "Woman of beautiful form." A female captive of war whom an Israelite soldier might wish to marry. The Torah prescribes specific procedures before such a marriage could take place (Deuteronomy 21:11-14).

Yibbum (יבום) - While not explicitly discussed in this chapter, the practice of levirate marriage relates to inheritance, as it ensures property remains within the family when a man dies without children. Referenced indirectly in discussion of inheritance practices.
Legal Terms and Commerce

Alah (אלה) - "Oath of curse" or "imprecation." A type of oath that involves a curse or penalty if broken. Distinguished from oaths by the Divine Name. Used in legal matters and disputes. Referenced in Numbers 5:21 regarding the suspected adulteress (Sotah).

Chabalah (חבלה) - "Pledge" or "collateral." Something taken as security for a loan. The Torah requires returning a poor person's garment taken as pledge before sunset, as it may be their only covering (Exodus 22:25-26).
Din (דין) - "Judgment" or "law." The process of legal decision-making based on Torah principles rather than rabbinic traditions. Referenced throughout the text when discussing legal matters.

Gevul (גבול) - "Boundary." Refers to property lines that must not be moved (Deuteronomy 19:14). The prohibition against moving a neighbor's boundary extends to any encroachment on another's property Lefts.

Marbit (מרבית) - "Interest." Taking additional payment beyond the principal of a loan. Distinguished from advance payment (neshekh). Prohibited when lending to fellow Israelites but permitted with foreigners (Deuteronomy 23:20-21).

Mechir Kelev (מחיר כלב) - "Price of a dog." Possibly referring to payment received for inappropriate sexual behavior or the fifty shekels fine for raping a virgin. Such money was not to be used for vows to God (Deuteronomy 23:18-19).

Neshekh (נשך) - "Usury" or "advance payment." Derived from "biting," referring to paying in advance for goods at a reduced price. Prohibited among Israelites but permitted with foreigners (Deuteronomy 23:20-21).

Nezek (נזק) - "Damage." Compensation required for injury caused to another person or their property. The text discusses various forms of damages requiring compensation, including "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (Exodus 21:24-25).

Shevuah (שבועה) - "Oath." The text discusses two primary types: oath by the Name (using God's name) and oath of curse or imprecation. Both are binding and carry serious consequences if broken (Exodus 20:7).

Yad (יד) - "Hand" in the sense of taking possession or responsibility. Used in discussions of theft and restoration of property. "Sending forth one's hand" (Exodus 22:7-8) refers to misappropriating a deposit.
Ritual Objects and Practices
Qiblah (קיבלה) - "Direction of prayer." For Karaites, prayer should be directed toward Jerusalem, based on Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:44, 48) and Daniel's practice (Daniel 6:11).

Techelet/Tekhelet (תכלת) - "Blue thread." Used in tzitzit (ritual fringes). While not extensively discussed in this excerpt, it's mentioned as part of Karaite ritual practice. The blue thread required in the tzitzit. Al-Qirqisani notes controversy over whether this refers to a specific substance, the color blue generally, or simply a color contrasting with the garment. Source: Numbers 15:38, "a thread of blue [techelet]."

Tzitzit (ציצית) - "Ritual fringes." The commandment to attach fringes to the corners of garments as a reminder of God's commandments. Al-Qirqisani notes debates about their composition and appearance. Source: Numbers 15:38, "and they shall put upon the fringe of each corner a thread of blue."
Sectarian Groups
Baytoum (ביתום) - A sectarian group mentioned in the text that supported determining the new month based on sighting the crescent in the west after sunset.

Cave Dwellers (אנשי המערות) - A group that claimed the full moon, not the crescent, should determine the beginning of the month, based on their understanding that the moon was created full. They cited Psalms 89:38: "like the moon shall be established forever."
Conjunctionists (מחברים) - Those who determined the new month based on the astronomical conjunction of the sun and moon rather than visual sighting.
Sadducees (צדוקים) - An ancient Jewish sect mentioned in the text as believing all months contain thirty days, citing the story of Noah where five months equaled 150 days.
Separatists (הנפרדים) - A sect mentioned that had different views on when to observe the new moon, possibly related to when the moon separates from the sun.

content.hebrew: {495} המאמר החמישי מספר האורות והמגדלים שעניינו ביאור מצוות התורה, חיברו יעקב בן יצחק אלקרקסאני.
content.english: {495} The Fifth Treatise of “The Book of Lights and Watchtowers,” an Explanation of the Torah’s Legal Commandments Authored by Jacob son of Isaac al-Qirqisani.

content.hebrew: ברוך אתה ה' למדני חוקיך.
content.english: “Blessed art Thou, O LORD; teach me Thy statutes.” (Psalms 119:12 )

content.hebrew: השער הראשון על אודות חובת המילה ביום השמיני.
content.english: The first gate regarding the obligation of circumcision on the eighth day.

content.hebrew: 1. האל ציווה את המצווה הזו לאברהם ומשה רבינו עליהם השלום והרחמים הזכיר אותה שוב. ובסיפור אברהם הזכיר בעניינה דברים שלא הזכיר משה משום שהוא קיצר ביחס לאמירה הראשונה עליה. והציון הראשון של זה הוא דברו לאברהם (בראשית יז:ט) 'ואתה את בריתי תשמור' ומה שבא אחריו (יז:י) 'זאת בריתי אשר תשמרו וג''. ואז אמר (שם שם) 'המול לכם כל זכר' ואז חזר על כך בדברו (יז:יא) 'ונמלתם את בשר ערלתכם'. וייתכן שדברו הראשון 'המול לכם כל זכר' הוא חיוב על כל מי שיש לו בן זכר שימול אותו, ודברו 'ונמלתם את בשר ערלתכם' הוא חיוב על האנשים הערלים להימול. ואז אמר (יז:יב) 'ובן שמונת ימים ימול לכם' והוא חייב זאת ביום השמיני ללידה. ואז אמר (שם שם) 'יליד בית ומקנת כסף' וכן חייב אותנו למול את עבדינו הנולדים [אצלנו] והנמכרים [לנו], אף אם הם אינם מחויבים בכלל הדת. הוא הודיע כי המילה היא ברית בינו וביננו וברית בבשרנו בדברו (יז:יא) 'והיה לאות ברית ביני וביניכם' (יז:יג) 'והיתה בריתי בבשרכם'. אנו לומדים משני פסוקים אלה כי סיבת החיוב במילה היא כדי שזו תהיה ברית בבשרנו וביננו ובין הבורא ישתבח. {498}
content.english: 1. God commanded this commandment to Abraham and repeated it to Moses, peace and mercy upon them. In the story of Abraham, are mentioned details not included in the story of Moses, because he condensed the first report regarding circumcision. For the first reference of circumcision to Abraham says (Genesis 17:9) “And God said unto Abraham: 'And as for thee, thou shalt keep My covenant, thou, and thy seed after thee throughout their generations.” and afterwards (Genesis 17:10) “This is My covenant, which ye shall keep, between Me and you and thy seed after thee: every male among you shall be circumcised.” Then he repeats this with the verse (Genesis 17:11) “And ye shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of a covenant between Me and you.” It is possible that his first verse “Every male among you shall be circumcised” is an obligation upon every one who has a male son to circumcise him, and his statement “And ye shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin” is an obligation upon uncircumcised men to be circumcised. Then he said (17:12) “And he that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you,” obligating this on the eighth day after birth. Then he said (ibid.) “he that is born in the house, or bought with money,” and he likewise obligated us to circumcise our slaves born [among us] and sold [to us], even though they are not obligated by religion as a whole. He informed [us] that circumcision is a covenant between Him and us and a covenant in our flesh through his statement (17:11) “and it shall be a token of a covenant between Me and you,” (17:13) “and My covenant shall be in your flesh.” We learn from these two verses that the reason for the obligation of circumcision is that this should be a covenant in our flesh between us and the Creator, may He be praised. {498}

content.hebrew: השער השני על אודות מה שמתחייב מי שלא נימול.
content.english: The second gate regarding the obligations of one who is not circumcised.

content.hebrew: 1. אחרי שהוא חייב את המילה בפסוקים רבים, ברורים ורצופים, הוא הדגיש רבות כי מי שלא נימול חייב מיתה. וזה בדברו (בראשית יז:יד) 'וערל זכר אשר לא ימול את בשר ערלתו ונכרתה הנפש ההיא מעמיה'. ואז הוא חזר והודיע לנו כי הסיבה לכך היא הברית וכאשר [האדם] מפר את הברית הוא מתחייב במיתה, וזה בדברו (יז:יד) 'את בריתי הפר'. כבר אמרנו לעיל כי השכל מונע שתחול חובת מיתה על בן שמונה ימים אם הוא אינו נימול, או שהוא יהיה זה שנדרש למול את עצמו, שכן זה חיוב שאין לסובלו ושבטלותו כבר הוכחה בראיות מופתיות. ודברו 'אשר לא ימול את בשר ערלתו ונכרתה' מתייחס אך ורק לבגיר שאינו נימול – אם הוא [בעל] מודעות עצמית ומודעות למצווה ובכל זאת הוא לא מל את עצמו הוא מחויב במיתה. ההיקש והשכל מחייבים גם הם מיתה על מי [שהוסמך] לקבל אחריות על עניינו [של הולד] מטעם האב או מטעם אדם אחר, אם הוא לא מל את התינוק ביום השמיני. 2. ואם יטען אדם כי [האדם] לא יתחייב [במיתה] אם הוא לא מל את התינוק ביום השמיני, אלא הוא יתחייב במיתה רק אם הוא לא ימול אותו בכלל, הרי טענה זו אינה מתקבלת על הדעת. זאת משום [שלפיה האדם] בהכרח לא ימות לעולם, שכן אם הוא לא מל ביום השמיני ואז נדרש למיתה, הוא יכול לומר שהוא ימול ביום התשיעי וכך הוא יינצל ממוות. וכן ביום העשירי ובזה שאחריו והוא תמיד יינצל, שכן בכל מצב ובכל יום הוא יכול לומר זאת בעת שהוא נדרש לכך והאמירה תיתן לו ארכה עד שהוא ימות. וזו בוודאי אינה כוונת הפסוק. חובת המיתה [עליו] מצאת היום השמיני אם הוא לא מקיים בו את המצווה היא ודאית, כל עוד זה לא קרה בגלל [שהוא היה אנוס להימנע מכך].
content.english: 1. After He obligated circumcision in many clear and consecutive versus, he emphasized that one who is uncircumcised is obligated in death as it says (Genesis 17:14) “And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people; he hath broken My covenant.'” Then He repeats with teachings that the reason for this is the covenant, and if one transgresses the covenant he is obligated in death. And this is derived from the verse (Genesis 17:14) “that soul shall be cut off from his people; he hath broken My covenant.” We already mentioned above that reason prevents us from concluding that a child who is uncircumcised past their eight day is obligated to be killed, or that he is obligated to circumcise himself, for such would be an impossible command for a child to fulfill and its unfulfillment is guaranteed. Thus, the verse (Genesis 17:14) “And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin” only applies to adults who are uncircumcised and who are self-conscious and aware of the commandment and still do not fulfill it, he is obligated with death. Indeed both reason and analogy both obligate death upon whomever is responsible for a child, whether his father or another person, to be circumcised on the eighth day and neglects this responsibility. 2. And if one were to argue that one is obligated to be killed only if he does not circumcise the child at all, and not merely for only missing the eight day, behold such an argument is not acceptable. For if such a view was correct, the individual responsible for the child would never be killed, for he could say on the eighth day I will circumcise him on the ninth day to save himself from death. And then on the ninth day, and each subsequent day, he can keep promising to circumcise the child the next day to save himself, and continue delaying until the day of his natural death. Clearly this is not what the verse intends, and the obligation of death certainly begins once the eighth day has concluded unless he has failed due to extenuating circumstances.

content.hebrew: השער השלישי על אודות [השאלה] האם יש חיוב למול מי שמת לפני היום השמיני או לא.
content.english: The third gate concerning whether it is obligatory to circumcise a child who died before the eight day.

content.hebrew: 1. הרבניים חייבו למול אותו כשהוא מת, ואף אחד מקרב אנשינו ומקרב הענניים ומכלל כיתות הקראים אינו מסכים לכך. אחד מהם שעוסק בעיון טוען בזכות חיוב הדבר בכך שהוא טען שהמקרא חייב את המצווה באופן כולל ולא {499} תלה את המצווה בחי או בזולתו. ואם כך הדבר, איננו יכולים להוציא את המת מכלל החובה כאשר המקרא לא הוציא אותו. בתגובה לכך יש לומר להם ראשית כי המקרא גם חייב שזה ייעשה ביום השמיני באופן כולל והוא לא הבחין בין אחד לאחר. אם כך עליכם להניח את המת, בין אם מת ביום הראשון או השני, עד ליום השמיני ואז תמולו אותו בשמיני על פי הציווי [המקראי]. ואם המילה בשמיני אינה חלה על המת אזי היא אינה חלה על המת אף בכל דרך [אחרת]. ואם יציעו סיבה [למה למול לפני היום השמיני] מצד הריקבון והקלקול שיידבקו במת עד היום השמיני, אין זה דבר שיכול לבטל את המצווה מכיון שאין בה יוצאי מן הכלל. הרי אפשר לטפל בריקבון ולתקן אותו באמצעות דברים שישמרו אותו מפני הקלקול במשך חמישה ימים ואף יותר, שכן דבר זה כבר נעשה באנשים והם שומרו במשך שנים כפי שנעשה לאדון [יוסף]. 2. בנוסף יש לומר להם שהבורא ישתבח ויתעלה אמר לנו (שמות לד:כ) 'ופטר חמור תפדה בשה ואם לא תפדה וערפתו' וכן אמר (שם שם) 'וכל בכור בניך תפדה'. דבר זה אינו תלוי בחי דווקא, אלא הוא חייב אותו חיוב כולל. ולכן, הם [הרבניים] צריכים להגיד שאם חמור מת לפני שהוא נפדה חובה לפדותו כשהוא מת כפי שחובה למול מת, וכך הדבר גם לגבי בני אדם. ואם יטענו כי המת אינו יכול להיפדות, יש לומר להם כי הוא גם אינו יכול להימול, ואין הבדל. באותה מידה מכריע כנגדם דברו (ויקרא כב:כז) 'שור או כשב או עז כי יולד והיה שבעת ימים תחת אמו'. אם הוא מת אחרי יומיים או שלושה מעת לידתו עליו להישאר אצל אימו עד תום שבעת ימים, שכן המקרא לא ייחד זאת לחי דווקא. ואם הם רוצים להבחין בין שני הפסוקים בכך שבזה נאמר (שמות כב:כט) 'וביום השמיני תתנו לי' [והבהמה] חייבת להישאר אצל אימה רק כדי שתהיה ראויה להיות לה' ביום השמיני, יש לומר להם: זהו ציווי שני [והוא אינו מכחיש את הראשון], ואילו הראשון עומד בפני עצמו והוא מחייב כפי שאתם טענתם לגבי מילה. בכל אופן, אפשר לטעון כנגדם גם באשר למילה, שכן אחרי שהוא אמר (בראשית יז:יא) 'ונמלתם את בשר ערלתכם' הוא אמר לגבי זה (שם שם) 'והיה לאות ברית' – במילה מחויב רק מי שזו תהיה אות ברית בבשרו, ואצל מת זה לא יהיה אות ברית, ואין הבדל [בעניין זה בין מילה ופדיון בהמה]. 3. ובאופן דומה מכריע כנגדם דברו (ויקרא יג:ב) 'אדם כי יהיה בעור בשרו שאת או ספחת' וכו', וכן דברו (שם ט) 'נגע צרעת כי תהיה באדם' וכו', וכן כל מה שהוא ממין זה – כל אלה אם מתו יש להביא אותם אל הכהן. ובכל עניין שהם רוצים ליצור בו הבחנה [כמקרה מיוחד השונה ממצוות המילה], כגון מילת המת ומה שמוזכר בה בנוגע לברית בבשר, טיעון דומה לזה יכריח כנגדם. וכך [הרבניים היו צריכים להגיד לפי שיטתם] גם בקשר לזב ולנדה וליולדה, אם מתו לפני שרחצו יש לרחצם ולהקריב קרבן עבור מי מהם שצריך להקריב. ויש עוד דוגמאות רבות אין ספור לדברים אשר יוכיחו נגדם. למשל, הזאת מי נדה על טמא מת אשר מת לפני תום שבעת הימים, וכן גילוח ראש המצורע ולקיחת שתי ציפורים חיות. ואם הם ייתלו בכך שזה אשר חייב {500} להימול הוא ילד שאינו חייב במצוות ולכן אדם אחר מחויב לקיים בו את המצווה, וזה האדם הבוגר, יש לשאול אותם על אודות בוגר שלא נימול. או אפשר להקשות עליהם מילד שנגע במת ואז מת [בעצמו], ולכן זה אשר אחראי עליו צריך להזות עליו מי נידה. ואם הם יאמרו כי יש להזות מי נידה רק כדי להיטהר בהם ואילו הילד המת איך ייטהר, שהרי טומאתו היא בדרגת הטומאה הגבוהה ביותר? יש לומר להם שהמטרה במילה היא רק שתהיה ברית בבשר ואילו למת אין ברית בבשרו. זאת ועוד יש לומר להם: האין אתם טוענים כי אם קרה לזב מקרה של קרי, הוא מוכרח לרחוץ במים כדי לקיים את המצווה, אף שהוא לא נטהר [בזה]? באותה המידה עליכם לחייב הזאת מי נדה על המת אף אם הוא אינו נטהר, ואין הבדל. 4. בנוסף יש לומר להם גם כן: אם מילת המת היא חובה שכן האל לא ייחד בכך את החי על פני זולתו [כלומר, המת], הם צריכים לומר אפוא שמי שנידון בשריפה או בסקילה ומת לפני שזה קרה לו, עליו להישרף או להיסקל אף על פי שהוא מת. ואם הם יאמרו כי השריפה והסקילה הם עונש והם חלים רק על החי, שכן איזה עונש ניתן להשית על המת, יש להקשות עליהם כדוגמת זאת מהברית שבמילה. זה יהיה כעצם בגרונם שכן כפי שכתבנו לעיל בשער השביעי במאמר הרביעי, לכל מצווה יש מטרה וסיבה וכאשר בטלה הסיבה בטל המסובב. ואם נכון הדבר שמטרת המילה והסיבה שלה היא הברית, אז כאשר בטל הברית בטלה המילה. וכדוגמת זאת מוכיח נגדם הפסוק (דברים כה:יב) 'וקצותה את כפה' וכן (שמות כא:ו) 'ורצע אדוניו את אזנו במרצע' וגילוח ראש הנזיר וכל מה שדומה לכך.
content.english: 1. The Rabbanites obligate circumcision upon one who died, and none of our companions, neither from the Ananites nor amongst any of the sects of the Qaraites, agrees with this. One of the Rabbanites who engages in speculation argues that this obligation is derived from the Torah’s description of circumcision in a general manner that does not {499} delimit circumcision to those alive and none else. If so, we cannot exclude the dead from the commandment of circumcision if the Torah did not do so. In response to this, we can point out first that the Torah also commands that circumcision be performed on the eight day without distinction. Thus, according to them, if a child dies on the first or second day, they should wait until the eighth day to circumcise him according to this commandment. However, if “eighth-day circumcision” does not apply to the dead, it follows that circumcision in all of its aspects does not apply to the dead. If they suggest that such a circumcision occur prior to the eighth day, such as the decomposition and rotting of the body, these considerations cannot cancel the general obligation for eighth-day circumcision that has no exceptions. For there are ways to preserve [the child’s corpse] until the eighth day or even beyond as is practiced in some communities for years, like was done with our Master, Joseph. 2. Furthermore, one must respond to them that the Creator, blessed and exalted, said to us (Exodus 34:20) “And the firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break its neck...” and also said (Exodus 34:20) “And all the firstborn of thy sons thou shalt redeem.” This too does not depend specifically on the living, but is rather an obligation in general terms. Therefore they [the Rabbanites] would have to say that if an ass dies before it has been redeemed, it is obligatory to redeem it while it is dead just as it is obligatory to circumcise the dead — and the same applies to human beings. And if they argue that the dead cannot be redeemed, say to them that neither can he be circumcised, and there is no difference. In the same manner, the verse (Leviticus 22:27) “When a bullock, or a sheep, or a goat, is brought forth, then it shall be seven days under the dam” refutes them. For if it dies two or three days after its birth, it must remain with its mother until the seven days are complete, since Scripture did not single out the living for this. And if they wish to distinguish between the two verses by saying that of this one it is said (Exodus 22:29) “and on the eighth day thou shalt give it Me,” and that [the animal] must remain with its dam only so as to be fit to be given to the LORD on the eighth day, say to them: this is a second command [which does not contradict the first], whereas the first stands on its own and is obligating in just the way you yourselves argued concerning circumcision. In any event, the same argument can be turned against them in the case of circumcision itself: for after he said (Genesis 17:11) “And ye shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin” he said concerning it (ibid.) “and it shall be a token of a covenant” — circumcision is obligatory only upon one in whose flesh it will become a token of a covenant, and in the case of the dead it will not be a token of a covenant, and there is no difference [in this matter between circumcision and the redemption of an animal]. 3. And similarly, the verse (Leviticus 13:2) “When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, or a scab” etc., and his statement (ibid. 9) “When the plague of leprosy is in a man” etc., and everything of this kind refutes them — for if any of these die they would [by their reasoning] have to be brought to the priest. In every matter in which they wish to draw a distinction [making it a special case differing from the commandment of circumcision], such as the circumcision of the dead and what is mentioned concerning it about the covenant in the flesh, an argument like this will refute them. And the same [the Rabbanites would have to say, on their own method] regarding the zav and the niddah and the parturient: if they died before being washed, they would have to be washed, and a sacrifice would have to be offered for any of them required to bring one. And there are still countless further examples that refute them. For instance: sprinkling waters of niddah upon one defiled by a corpse who himself died before the seven days were complete; and the shaving of the leper’s head and the taking of two living birds. And if they hang their argument on the claim that the one obligated {500} to be circumcised is a child who is not himself bound by the commandments, and that therefore some other person — the adult — is obligated to fulfill the commandment upon him, ask them about an adult who has not been circumcised. Or one may press them with the case of a child who touched a corpse and then died himself, in which case the one responsible for him must sprinkle waters of niddah upon him. And if they say that waters of niddah are sprinkled only to purify with them, and that the dead child — how can he be purified, since his impurity is of the highest grade? — say to them: the aim in circumcision is only that there be a covenant in the flesh, and the dead has no covenant in his flesh. Furthermore, say to them: do you not maintain that if an emission befalls a zav, he is required to bathe in water in order to fulfill the commandment, even though he is not [thereby] purified? In the same manner you must obligate sprinkling waters of niddah upon the dead even though he is not purified, and there is no difference. 4. Furthermore, say to them also: if circumcising the dead is obligatory, on the grounds that God did not single out in this the living over anyone else [i.e., over the dead], they must accordingly say that one sentenced to burning or stoning who dies before the sentence is carried out upon him must be burned or stoned even though he is dead. And if they reply that burning and stoning are punishments and apply only to the living — for what punishment can be imposed upon the dead? — the same kind of objection must be pressed against them from the covenant of circumcision. This will be as a bone in their throats; for as we have written above, in the seventh gate of the fourth Discourse, every commandment has a purpose and a reason, and when the reason is voided the consequent is voided. And if it is correct that the purpose of circumcision, and the reason for it, is the covenant, then when the covenant is voided the circumcision is voided. And similarly the verse (Deuteronomy 25:12) “then thou shalt cut off her hand” refutes them, and likewise (Exodus 21:6) “and his master shall bore his ear through with an awl,” and the shaving of the nazirite’s head, and everything of this sort.

content.hebrew: השער הרביעי על אודות מילת הבגיר, הגר והעבד הנקנה, מתי העת הנכונה לכך.
content.english: The fourth gate concerning the timing of circumcising adults, converts, and purchased slaves.
